items.title: 3.10 A comparison among ionic, covalent, metallic bonds and intermolecular forces

source_refs.note: Topic 3.10, printed page 69 (Table 3.4, printed four times). The text's hydrogen bond value (20 to 25) differs from the table's (20 to 50); both are recorded.

blocks.text: Chemical bonds, that is ionic, covalent and metallic bonds, are usually termed true chemical bonds because they affect the chemical properties of a substance: they result in the formation of new species through the transfer and sharing of electrons, whereas intermolecular forces act to bring molecules closer and influence the physical properties. Such a clear distinction is not always possible, however. The distinctive feature of chemical bonds and intermolecular forces is their bond strength, measured by the bond energy.

The bond energy of the ionic bond in sodium chloride (760 kJ per mol) is the highest, followed by the covalent bond (O-H, 464 kJ per mol) and the average hydrogen bond (20 to 25 kJ per mol). This shows that the ionic bond is the strongest form of chemical bonding and that chemical bonds are generally much stronger than intermolecular forces. The permanent dipole-dipole forces (5 to 20 kJ per mol) and London dispersion forces (1 to 20 kJ per mol) are weaker still. The metallic bond is mostly explained by electrostatic forces, although some theories suggest it may be covalent in nature; in any case it is weaker than both the ionic and the covalent bond, with an average bond energy of 100 to 150 kJ per mol, and a satisfactory reason for its low strength is the extensive delocalization of electrons within the metallic crystal.

blocks.prompt: Why is the metallic bond weaker than the ionic and covalent bonds, and why are ionic, covalent and metallic bonds called true chemical bonds while van der Waals forces are not?
blocks.explanation: In a metal the valence electrons are delocalized over the whole crystal rather than held between particular atoms, so the attraction is spread thin and the average bond energy is only 100 to 150 kJ per mol. Ionic, covalent and metallic bonds form new species by transferring or sharing electrons and decide chemical properties; intermolecular forces only draw existing molecules together, affect physical properties, and are far weaker (1 to 50 kJ per mol).

items: True chemical bonds (ionic, covalent, metallic) make new species and set chemical properties; intermolecular forces draw molecules together and set physical properties. Strength by bond energy: NaCl ionic 760 > O-H covalent 464 > metallic 100 to 150 > hydrogen bond 20 to 50 > dipole-dipole 5 to 20 > van der Waals 1 to 20 kJ per mol.
